Empirical Research Plan:  Minimum-Wage Increase and Fast-Food Employment  
(New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania, early-1990s episode)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID), complemented by an event-study (dynamic DID) to examine pre-trends.

Why appropriate  
• Policy variation is discrete, dateable, and applies to all fast-food restaurants in one state but not the other.  
• We observe two groups (NJ = treated, PA = control) both before and after the policy.  
• Restaurant-level panel (or repeated cross-section) allows us to difference out time-invariant group factors and common macro shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Treat_i = 1 if restaurant i is located in New Jersey, 0 if Pennsylvania.

Control group  
  Fast-food restaurants in Pennsylvania, which faced an unchanged federal minimum wage.

Treatment timing  
  Event date: 1 April 1992 (the day the NJ state minimum wage rose from \$4.25 to \$5.05).  
  Post_t = 1 for observations dated on/after April-1992 survey; 0 otherwise.

Running variable / cutoff  
  Not applicable (not an RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the NJ hike, the employment trajectory at NJ and PA fast-food restaurants would have been the same.  
  Plausibility: Neighboring states share macro conditions; pre-policy months can be checked graphically and with placebo regressions.

A2. No spillovers / interference (SUTVA): PA restaurants are unaffected by NJ’s higher minimum.  
  Plausibility: Most PA stores are far enough from the border, but cross-border labor flows could dilute treatment; we will test for border effects.

A3. Stable composition: Entry/exit of restaurants is not systematically differentially affected in the short window we study.  
  Plausibility: Six-to-eight-month horizon limits exit/entry; we can balance panels and test attrition.

A4. No other contemporaneous state-specific shocks: No PA-vs-NJ policy changes coincident with 1-Apr-1992 affecting fast-food labor demand.  
  Plausibility: We will search newspapers / legislative records; include county-level controls.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends  
  • Mitigation: Event-study coefficients for –6, –5, –4, … months; include leads of treatment. Falsify if pre-coefficients ≈ 0.  
  • Restrict to balanced panel to avoid composition differences over time.

T2. Cross-state worker commuting / spillovers  
  • Mitigation: Drop/rest test restaurants within 10 or 20 miles of the state border; re-estimate.  
  • If results differ, report both full-sample and “interior-county” estimates.

T3. Measurement error in employment (survey vs phone)  
  • Mitigation: Instrument with number of cash registers or seating capacity (if available) to proxy true store size; robustness to using full-time-equivalent rather than headcount.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
#-------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # TWFE and event study
library(did)            # Callaway–Sant’Anna, if staggered (optional)
library(ggplot2)

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load Data
#-------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("fastfood_nj_pa_1991_1992.csv")   # placeholder file name

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable Construction
#-------------------------------------------------------
# basic identifiers
dt[, treat  := ifelse(state == "NJ", 1, 0)]
dt[, post   := ifelse(date >= as.Date("1992-04-01"), 1, 0)]
dt[, did    := treat * post]

# Panel identifiers
dt[, store_id := .GRP, by = .(chain, address)]   # if id not provided

# Event-study periods (monthly bins, –6 .. +6 relative to April-1992)
dt[, rel_month := as.integer(12*(year(date) - 1992) + month(date) - 4)]
dt[, rel_month := pmax(pmin(rel_month, 6), -6)]   # clamp tails

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main DID Regression
#-------------------------------------------------------
est_main <- feols(employment ~ treat*post | store_id + month_year, 
                  data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(est_main)

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Event-Study
#-------------------------------------------------------
dt[, leadlag := i(rel_month)]
event_spec <- feols(employment ~ i(rel_month, treat, ref = -1) | 
                    store_id + month_year, cluster = ~state, data = dt)
iplot(event_spec)  # confidence-interval plot of dynamic effects

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness:  drop border counties
#-------------------------------------------------------
border_counties <- c("Burlington","Camden","Gloucester",     # example
                     "Delaware","Chester","Philadelphia")
dt_rb <- dt[!(county %in% border_counties)]
est_rb <- feols(employment ~ treat*post | store_id + month_year,
                data = dt_rb, cluster = ~state)
etable(est_main, est_rb, se="cluster")

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Heterogeneity: By chain (McD vs BK vs KFC)
#-------------------------------------------------------
est_chain <- feols(employment ~ treat*post:chain | store_id + month_year,
                   data = dt, cluster = ~state)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior from competitive-labor-market theory: A binding minimum wage should lower employment (negative β).  
Magnitude guess: −0.10 to −0.20 FTE workers per restaurant (≈ 2–4 % of baseline headcount).  
However, prior empirical findings (incl. monopsony models) suggest effect could be near zero or slightly positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually & statistically verified ..... 0.8  
C2: No contemporaneous confounders ..................................... 0.7  
C3: No spillovers / interference (SUTVA) ................................ 0.6  
C4: Consistent treatment assignment & timing ............................ 1.0  
C5: Robustness across specifications / samples .......................... 0.8  

(Overall average ≈ 0.78 → credible but not bullet-proof.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
